SolarInfo.quyDaoTronDongPhangPhaKhoiDauT: Circular, coplanar orbits with illustrative starting phases, not current astronomical positions. Rotation uses the same simulated days; axis orientations and prime meridians are illustrative.
SolarInfo.beMatMayKhiQuyenVaVanhDaiDuoc: Surfaces, clouds, atmospheres and rings are generated procedurally, not NASA photographs or measured terrain maps. Rings lie in the equatorial plane; widths and gaps are illustrative. Spheres use mean radii without modeling oblateness.

bodies.sun.name: Sun
bodies.sun.description: The self-luminous star at the center of the Solar System. Planets reflect sunlight.
bodies.mercury.name: Mercury
bodies.mercury.description: The closest planet to the Sun. Its rocky surface is heavily cratered and lacks thick clouds like those of Venus.
bodies.venus.name: Venus
bodies.venus.description: Thick clouds hide the surface. The model's creamy yellow represents the clouds, not a photograph of the planet's surface.
bodies.earth.name: Earth
bodies.earth.description: Our planet, with oceans, continents and an atmosphere. The Moon is Earth's natural satellite.
bodies.mars.name: Mars
bodies.mars.description: A rocky planet with reddish-brown hues from iron-bearing minerals. The model illustrates terrain regions and bright polar caps.
bodies.jupiter.name: Jupiter
bodies.jupiter.description: The Solar System's largest planet. Cloud bands and the Great Red Spot are procedural illustrations, not photographs.
bodies.saturn.name: Saturn
bodies.saturn.description: A gas giant with thin rings in its equatorial plane. Gaps between the illustrated rings are schematic.
bodies.uranus.name: Uranus
bodies.uranus.description: A pale cyan ice giant. Its rotation axis is tilted about 97.77° from the orbital normal, almost on its side.
bodies.neptune.name: Neptune
bodies.neptune.description: The outermost of the eight planets, an ice giant. The gentle blue is illustrative; saturated blue in some enhanced images is not treated as a measured color.
bodies.moon.name: Moon
bodies.moon.description: Earth's natural satellite, not a planet or star. Dark plains and craters in the model are illustrative.
stars.sun.name: Sun
stars.sun.description: Our star. The Sun is a sphere of hot plasma, providing light and energy for life on Earth.
stars.sun.facts.1: Located in the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic center.
stars.sun.facts.2: Energy is produced by nuclear fusion in the core.
stars.sun.note: Physical values are rounded for education. The Sun is the origin in the neighborhood scene; its galactic marker shows an illustrative relative position.
stars.sirius-a.name: Sirius A
stars.sirius-a.description: The bright component of the Sirius binary system. It is a prominent bright star in Earth's night sky.
stars.sirius-a.facts.0: Sirius B is a white dwarf companion, not drawn separately at this scale.
stars.sirius-a.facts.1: Apparent brightness depends on both intrinsic luminosity and distance.
stars.sirius-a.note: ICRS coordinates at epoch J2000 and parallax 379.21 mas from SIMBAD/Hipparcos (2007). Distance is calculated from parallax and rounded; proper motion is not updated.
stars.vega.name: Vega
stars.vega.description: Known in East Asian tradition as the weaving star. Vega is one of the three vertices of the Summer Triangle.
stars.vega.facts.0: Forms the Summer Triangle with Altair and Deneb.
stars.vega.facts.1: A pattern in the sky does not mean the stars are close together in space.
stars.vega.note: ICRS coordinates at epoch J2000 and parallax 130.23 mas from SIMBAD/Hipparcos (2007). Type A0 V is from the SIMBAD record citing 2024A&A...690A.176N.
stars.altair.name: Altair
stars.altair.description: Known as the cowherd star in East Asian tradition, Altair is a vertex of the Summer Triangle.
stars.altair.facts.0: Seen from Earth, Altair and Vega lie on opposite sides of the Milky Way band.
stars.altair.facts.1: Familiar star names connect astronomy with culture.
stars.altair.note: ICRS coordinates at epoch J2000 and parallax 194.95 mas from SIMBAD/Hipparcos (2007). Distance uses inverse parallax, appropriate for illustrating this nearby star.
stars.barnard.name: Barnard’s Star
stars.barnard.description: A red dwarf near the Sun, famous for its very large proper motion across the sky.
stars.barnard.facts.0: Not visible to the naked eye.
stars.barnard.facts.1: Its position is held at epoch J2000, not updated in real time.
stars.barnard.note: ICRS coordinates at epoch J2000 and parallax 546.9759 mas from the SIMBAD record citing Gaia EDR3 (2020).
stars.proxima.name: Proxima Centauri
stars.proxima.description: The nearest star to the Solar System, a faint red dwarf in the Alpha Centauri system.
stars.proxima.facts.0: Light takes more than four years to travel from Proxima to us.
stars.proxima.facts.1: Despite being so close, it is not visible to the naked eye.
stars.proxima.note: Approximate distance for education. Coordinates of the star itself: ICRS, epoch J2000 from SIMBAD citing Gaia EDR3 (2020). Proper motion is not simulated.
stars.alpha-centauri.name: Alpha Centauri AB
stars.alpha-centauri.description: The A and B pair in the Alpha Centauri system. This record represents AB; Proxima Centauri (component C) has its own record.
stars.alpha-centauri.facts.0: The parameters of the two stars are not combined into a fictitious single star.
stars.alpha-centauri.facts.1: At a light-year scale, the separation of A and B is very small.
stars.alpha-centauri.note: Reference record; unverified parameters are left blank. No verified coordinates are available in this version, so only information is shown.
stars.trappist.name: TRAPPIST-1
stars.trappist.description: An ultracool dwarf with seven roughly Earth-sized planets, an important target for exoplanet research.
stars.trappist.facts.0: Seven planets orbit one small star.
stars.trappist.facts.1: A planet's Earth-like size does not mean Earth-like conditions for life.
stars.trappist.note: Approximate distance for education. Coordinates have not been verified; information only.
stars.betelgeuse.name: Betelgeuse
stars.betelgeuse.description: A prominent red supergiant at Orion's shoulder. Its brightness and size change over time.
stars.betelgeuse.facts.0: Its distance and radius have substantial uncertainties.
stars.betelgeuse.facts.1: This model cannot predict exactly when a star will explode.
stars.betelgeuse.note: Reference record; unverified parameters are left blank. No verified coordinates are available in this version, so only information is shown.
stars.rigel.name: Rigel
stars.rigel.description: The bright blue supergiant component of the Rigel system, toward Orion's foot.
stars.rigel.facts.0: A blue hue suggests a hotter surface than that of red stars.
stars.rigel.facts.1: A stellar system may contain several components that cannot be resolved with the naked eye.
stars.rigel.note: Reference record; unverified parameters are left blank. No verified coordinates are available in this version, so only information is shown.
stars.polaris.name: Polaris
stars.polaris.description: A stellar system currently near the north celestial pole. Its main component is a Cepheid variable.
stars.polaris.facts.0: It is not the brightest star in the sky.
stars.polaris.facts.1: The role of pole star changes over long periods because of Earth's precession.
stars.polaris.note: Reference record; unverified parameters are left blank. No verified coordinates are available in this version, so only information is shown.
stars.deneb.name: Deneb
stars.deneb.description: A luminous supergiant at the tail of Cygnus, forming the third vertex of the Summer Triangle.
stars.deneb.facts.0: Much farther away than Vega and Altair.
stars.deneb.facts.1: Brightness in the sky does not directly tell us distance.
stars.deneb.note: Reference record; unverified parameters are left blank. No verified coordinates are available in this version, so only information is shown.
lessons.galaxy.title: What is the Milky Way?
lessons.galaxy.text: The Milky Way is the galaxy containing our Solar System: a huge collection of stars, gas, dust and dark matter bound by gravity. It is a barred spiral galaxy. The bright band in our sky is our view from inside its disk, like standing in a forest and looking along the tree trunks.
lessons.location.title: Where are we?
lessons.location.text: The Solar System lies in the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the Milky Way's center. We are not at the center of the galaxy. The yellow marker shows the Solar System's relative position; the model's rotation and arms are illustrative.
lessons.lightYear.title: How far is a light-year?
lessons.lightYear.text: A light-year is a unit of distance: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 trillion km. Light from Proxima Centauri takes more than four years to reach us. When you look at a star, you see its past.
lessons.starColors.title: Why do stars have different colors?
lessons.starColors.text: Stellar color relates to surface temperature. Hotter stars tend to be blue-white; cooler stars tend to be orange-red, much as heated metal changes from red to white-hot. Screen colors are illustrative cues, not spectral measurements.
lessons.categories.title: Star, planet, moon or galaxy?
lessons.categories.text: Stars produce their own energy through nuclear fusion for most of their lives: the Sun and Sirius are stars. Planets orbit stars and reflect light: Earth and Jupiter are planets. Natural satellites orbit planets: the Moon orbits Earth. Galaxies contain stars, gas, dust and other components: the Milky Way is a galaxy. Vietnamese planet names such as “Sao Mộc” include a word for star, but Jupiter is a planet.
lessons.scales.title: Why use different scales?
lessons.scales.text: The galactic view uses 1 unit = 1,000 light-years; the neighborhood uses 1 unit = 1 light-year. The Solar System is much smaller: Explore adjusts radii and distances independently. Size comparison uses one linear radius scale; side-by-side positions are not orbits. Orbital distance mode uses one AU scale but enlarges model radii. 1 AU is 149,597,870.7 km. Profile values are physical data, not measurements from the transformed model.
scales.explore: Explore: planetary radii are enlarged relative to the Sun with nonlinear compression; distances preserve order, not true scale. Do not measure data from the image.
scales.size: Comparison: all radii share one linear scale — 1 unit = 10,000 km. Side-by-side positions compare sizes, not orbital distances. Locators are not radii.
scales.distance: Orbits: 10 units = 1 AU, using one linear distance scale based on semi-major axes. Model radii are enlarged independently; the Moon may overlap Earth at this scale.

phen.intro.blackhole: A non-rotating black hole: explore its boundary, exterior matter and optional accretion disk.
phen.intro.solarEclipse: The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. Compare the shadow with the sky at the green observer.
phen.intro.lunarEclipse: Earth is in the middle. Follow the Moon through Earth’s penumbra and umbra.
phen.intro.tides: Two tidal bulges, an observer rotating with Earth, and a graph computed from the same model.

phen.fallback: WebGL is unavailable. The 2D diagram, timeline and explanations still share the same simulation state.
phen.notToScale: Diagram not to scale. Earth radius used in calculations: {{earth}} km.
phen.observerDiagram: Observer view and overlap computed from the model
phen.graph.title: Relative water level at the green observer
phen.graph.aria: Equilibrium tide graph over one rotation, illustrative units
phen.supernova.structure: Colored layers schematically represent a massive star before collapse. Enable the cutaway to reveal its bright core.
phen.supernova.collapse: When pressure support is insufficient, the core collapses rapidly. This illustrates contraction, without solving hydrodynamics or neutrino transport.
phen.supernova.shock: The gold wire shell marks the shock front; orange particles represent expelled matter. The brightening represents radiation, not particles moving at light speed.
phen.supernova.remnant: Ejecta continue to expand. This scenario leaves a neutron star; other outcomes depend on the progenitor and collapse process.
phen.blackhole.horizon: Inside the event horizon, light cannot escape outward. The black sphere and blue grid mark a boundary, not a solid surface.
phen.blackhole.disk: The luminous disk is outside the horizon. Switch it off: an isolated black hole need not have a bright accretion disk.
phen.blackhole.matter: Dots outside the boundary move on illustrative orbits. A black hole does not automatically vacuum up everything around it.
phen.blackhole.light: Enable light paths to see schematic bent curves. They are not general-relativistic ray tracing or a simulated black-hole shadow image.
phen.solarEclipse.none: At the observer, the disks have not overlapped or have moved apart. Solar eclipses require close alignment near new Moon.
phen.solarEclipse.partial: The Moon covers part of the Sun at the green observer. This classification applies to that location, not everywhere on Earth.
phen.solarEclipse.total: The Moon’s angular size and alignment cover the entire solar disk at the green observer, inside the Moon’s umbra.
phen.solarEclipse.annular: The more distant Moon appears smaller than the Sun. The observer lies beyond the umbral apex, in the antumbra, leaving a bright ring.
phen.lunarEclipse.none: The Moon is outside the shadows. A lunar eclipse needs full-Moon alignment near an orbital node, not merely any full Moon.
phen.lunarEclipse.penumbral: The Moon enters only the penumbra, where Earth blocks part of the light source. Dimming is subtle; its area inside the umbra remains zero.
phen.lunarEclipse.partial: Part of the Moon enters Earth’s umbra. This is Earth’s shadow, not the day–night boundary responsible for ordinary lunar phases.
phen.lunarEclipse.total: The entire lunar disk is inside the umbra. In reality, sunlight filtered through Earth’s atmosphere can make it look red; the Moon does not emit its own light.
phen.tides.spring: Sun, Earth and Moon are aligned. Their tidal contributions reinforce, increasing relative range as the rotating observer passes high and low regions.
phen.tides.neap: The solar and lunar directions are nearly perpendicular. Their contributions partially cancel, reducing range. Toggle the Sun’s contribution to compare the same model.
phen.limit.supernova: Only a massive-star core-collapse scenario, not all supernova types. Size, time and brightness are adjusted; layers, shock and particles are not hydrodynamic solutions. The neutron star is one illustrative outcome, not a universal result.
phen.limit.blackhole: A non-rotating black hole. The grid marks the horizon, not the observed shadow. The disk is outside it; orbits and light curves are schematic, without a general-relativistic solver. No jets or escaping light are drawn from inside the horizon.
phen.limit.solarEclipse: Overlap uses physical radii and positions in km, independently of compressed display distances and sizes. The overview is not to one scale; shadow cones use paraxial geometry. Preset tracks are not an ephemeris. Lunar orbital tilt prevents eclipses at every new Moon.
phen.limit.lunarEclipse: Umbra and penumbra come from Sun–Earth–Moon geometry before display scaling. Red is an illustrative material transition, not atmospheric radiative transfer. This is neither a lunar-phase simulation nor an actual eclipse prediction.
phen.limit.tides: A quadrupole equilibrium tide: contributions scale as M/d³ with P₂(cos θ). The ocean shell is exaggerated; the graph uses the same function in illustrative units, not meters. Coastlines, depth, lag and ocean dynamics are omitted. Do not use it to predict real tide times or heights.
phen.eyeSafety: For real solar viewing, use suitable ISO 12312-2 solar viewers or safe indirect projection; ordinary sunglasses do not protect your eyes.
phen.component.core.name: Stellar core
phen.component.core.text: The hot, dense center before collapse. The cutaway shows schematic layers, not measured sections or a detailed chemical calculation.
phen.component.envelope.name: Outer stellar matter
phen.component.envelope.text: Initially the layers around the core; after the shock, particles represent expanding matter. They are not the photons of the light flash.
phen.component.shock.name: Shock front
phen.component.shock.text: The gold wire shell marks a wave through matter, distinct from orange ejecta. Its displayed speed and thickness serve the explanation.
phen.component.neutron.name: Illustrative neutron star
phen.component.neutron.text: The compact core remnant chosen for this scenario. Not every supernova makes a neutron star or black hole; outcomes depend on the progenitor and collapse.
phen.component.horizon.name: Event horizon
phen.component.horizon.text: A causal boundary, not a solid shell. An observed black-hole shadow also involves light bending and capture, so it is not identical to the boundary sphere drawn here.
phen.component.disk.name: Accretion disk
phen.component.disk.text: Luminous matter outside the horizon. This non-rotating illustration places its inner edge at three horizon radii. The disk is optional; not every black hole has a bright gas supply.
phen.component.matter.name: Exterior matter
phen.component.matter.text: Particles follow schematic orbits outside the boundary and inner disk edge. These are not relativistic orbit solutions, nor a claim that all matter falls in.
phen.component.light.name: Illustrative light paths
phen.component.light.text: Blue curves suggest deflection of light. This version has no null-geodesic solver or accurate lensing image.
phen.component.sun.name: Sun
phen.component.sun.text: The light source for eclipses and one source of tides. Visible size and distance are adjusted; calculations use separate physical parameters.
phen.component.earth.name: Earth
phen.component.earth.text: Home to the observer and ocean layer. Earth blocks sunlight in lunar eclipses; the Moon’s shadow reaches Earth in solar eclipses.
phen.component.moon.name: Moon
phen.component.moon.text: A satellite reflecting sunlight, not generating its own light. Its position and radius participate in eclipse geometry and tidal calculations.
phen.component.umbra.name: Umbra
phen.component.umbra.text: The geometric region where the occulter covers the whole light source. In reality, Earth’s atmosphere can still send reddish sunlight into its umbra toward the Moon.
phen.component.penumbra.name: Penumbra
phen.component.penumbra.text: The occulter blocks only part of the light source. A penumbral lunar eclipse causes subtle dimming rather than a sharply darkened umbral region.
phen.component.antumbra.name: Antumbra
phen.component.antumbra.text: Beyond the umbral apex, the occulter appears smaller than the source. An observer can see a ring of the Sun around the Moon.
phen.component.observer.name: Observer
phen.component.observer.text: The green dot marks the sampling location. The solar sky view uses this observer; in tides it rotates with Earth, and the graph samples the same direction.
phen.component.water.name: Equilibrium ocean shell
phen.component.water.text: Tides arise from gravitational acceleration differences relative to Earth’s center. The quadrupole potential has opposite bulges rather than pulling all water to one side. Deformation is exaggerated, not a real height.
phen.component.forces.name: Tidal force
phen.component.forces.text: Arrows show acceleration relative to Earth’s center in a leading-order approximation. They are not the Moon’s full attraction or ocean currents.

phen.tides.lunarOnly: The Sun’s tidal contribution is off. The shell and graph contain only the lunar contribution; changing the configuration now rotates the two bulges without creating a spring–neap range difference.
